subtype: Approach: taking the conversation to private channels [Action]
passage: It was past eleven, the festival sale was live, and the support desk of a spice-delivery firm was down to Alka and one intern. A public post read: 'Order arrived with a torn box, no one replies, refund now.' Alka knew sorting it out meant sharing an order number and an address, and a public thread was no place for that. She replied, 'So sorry about the torn box. Could you email us, or tell us a good time for a call? We'll sort it today.' The customer wrote back within minutes and phoned at midnight. Alka arranged a replacement for the damaged item. Next morning she returned to the thread: 'Resolved with the customer directly. Thank you for flagging it.' Nitin from packing was asked to check the box tape.

qa.q: What did Alka ask the customer to do in the public reply?
qa.a: Alka asked the customer to email, or to name a good time for a call.

qa.q: What was Alka worried about in moving the complaint off the public thread?
qa.a: Alka was concerned about privacy, since sorting out the order meant sharing an order number and an address.

qa.q: What could Alka do if the customer refused to leave the public thread?
qa.a: Alka could post a short public note that an offer was made and stay available, keeping the details general.

qa.q: How might the customer have felt when the reply came so quickly?
qa.a: The customer probably felt relieved and heard, having written back within minutes and then phoned.

grounding: Shows a company moving a customer-specific complaint to a direct call or email and later saying publicly that it was resolved.

subtype: Approach: ignoring everything and hoping it fades [Pitfall]
passage: A rider's post appeared on Friday evening: the front brake on scooter 214 felt spongy and had nearly failed on a slope. Devika, who runs the scooter-rental firm in Pune, saw it and chose not to reply. 'It'll be buried by the weekend,' she told Ankita from operations. Ankita, uneasy, said that scooter should at least be pulled and checked, and that night marked it 'do not rent' without being asked. Devika still would not answer publicly. By Sunday six more riders had posted their own close calls. On Monday a local news page shared the thread under the line 'The company says nothing.' Phones at the office rang all morning, and Devika finally called an all-hands.

qa.q: Which scooter had the spongy brake?
qa.a: Scooter 214 had the spongy front brake.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel about the silence?
qa.a: Ankita felt uneasy, which is why Ankita marked the scooter 'do not rent' that night without being asked.

qa.q: What could Devika have done differently on Friday?
qa.a: Devika could have replied the same day, thanked the rider, said the scooter was pulled for checking, and named when an update would come.

qa.q: How might riders reading the silence have seen the company?
qa.a: They probably saw a company that did not care about safety, which is why more riders joined in.

grounding: Shows a company staying silent about a real safety complaint, so more users join in and a local matter becomes a wider reputation problem.

subtype: Approach: seeking a trusted friend's view [Action]
passage: At a café table in Addis Ababa, Abebe turned a laptop toward Clara, a friend. A reviewer on a travel forum had called Abebe's guesthouse 'dirty, with rude staff', and Abebe had written a reply overnight. 'Read it as if you don't know me,' Abebe said. Clara, who had never stayed there and had nothing riding on it, read slowly. 'The third line is sarcastic: "Sorry our standards weren't luxury enough for you." Take it out. And you never say what you'll do.' Abebe winced, then nodded. Together they cut the sarcasm and added a promise: 'We've changed the cleaning checklist, and I'll message you directly.' Abebe read it once more, said, 'That sounds like me on a good day,' and posted it before lunch.

qa.q: Which line did Clara say to take out?
qa.a: Clara said to take out the sarcastic third line, 'Sorry our standards weren't luxury enough for you.'

qa.q: How did Abebe feel about Clara's comment on the sarcasm, and what shows it?
qa.a: Abebe winced and then nodded, stung at first but ready to accept it.

qa.q: What could Abebe have done if no friend was free to read the draft?
qa.a: Abebe could have waited a day before posting, since overnight anger fades and a calmer reading shows the sarcasm.

qa.q: How might the reviewer see the final reply?
qa.a: The reviewer would probably feel heard, since the reply promised a change and a direct message and did not mock. 🙂

grounding: Shows a person sharing a draft reply with a friend who is not emotionally involved, who suggests removing sarcasm and adding a concrete promise.

subtype: Approach: protecting mental health while the storm passes [Thinking]
passage: Saturday. Day one of no notifications. A big page mocked my video and the comments have been ugly, and yesterday I checked the numbers every hour and felt sick each time. Today I muted everything for two days and left the phone in the drawer. Went to the market with Amma, then sat on the balcony with my sister Himani while she peeled peas, and I told her the worst comment. She said, 'Who wrote it? A stranger who won't remember you next week.' That helped more than I expected. I keep telling myself attention moves on and that what people I've never met say isn't the measure of me. Still stings a bit. I'll look on Monday, once. — Bhupen

qa.q: For how long did Bhupen mute notifications?
qa.a: Bhupen muted them for two days.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel when checking the numbers every hour?
qa.a: Bhupen felt sick each time, and now feels calmer though it still stings a bit.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do if the mocking carries on for longer?
qa.a: Bhupen could ask Himani or another trusted person to watch for real problems and mention only what needs an answer.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt hearing the worst comment?
qa.a: Himani was probably concerned and wanted to reassure, reminding Bhupen that a stranger would not remember it next week.

grounding: Shows a person muting notifications, avoiding hourly checks and talking with family while reminding themselves that strangers do not define their worth.

subtype: Approach: using legal remedies only for real harm [Revision]
passage: In the waiting room of a community legal advice centre, Simran sat with a folder of printed screenshots. Weeks earlier, some posts had claimed her bakery used spoiled flour and made customers ill. That was false, and it had cost her orders. Other posts only called her cakes dry and overpriced. In the first angry week she had drafted a message threatening every critic; she deleted it, seeing that honest dislike is not harm. Maria, the volunteer at the desk, glanced at the folder as Simran said, 'I sorted them. These four are false and hurt my shop. The rest are just people who didn't like the cakes, and I won't touch those.' Each page had a date and a link noted on it. Inside, she asked only about the false claims and what lawful options existed.

qa.q: How many posts did Simran count as false and harmful?
qa.a: Simran counted four posts as false and harmful.

qa.q: What did Simran realise when deleting the threatening draft?
qa.a: Simran realised her anger had run ahead of her: honest dislike of her cakes was not harm and did not deserve a threat.

qa.q: What other approach could Simran use for the honest critics?
qa.a: Simran could reply politely to honest criticism and use the platform's report tool for the false claims, since that answers fairness with fairness.

qa.q: How might the honest critics have felt if Simran had threatened them all?
qa.a: They would probably have felt bullied and more likely to spread the story, turning a small dislike into a bigger fight.

grounding: Shows a person collecting evidence of false and harmful posts and asking about lawful options, while not threatening critics for honest disagreement.

subtype: Approach: updating the product and process after the episode [Revision]
passage: Note from the team's coach, after the retrospective on the online complaint. I watched the team of six go quiet at first, then turn practical. Pallavi pointed out that most of the angry posts had begun as messages nobody could find a place to send. So the team agreed three changes: a short form for support linked inside the app, a changelog page anyone can read, and a target of answering every message the same working day. Pallavi sketched the form fields on the board. Anand, the product lead, asked that the changelog also list what was not fixed yet. I asked them to review the reply times in a month. They put the date in the calendar before leaving.

qa.q: What three changes did the team agree?
qa.a: They agreed a support form inside the app, a changelog page anyone can read, and answering every message the same working day.

qa.q: What did Pallavi think was behind most of the angry posts?
qa.a: Pallavi thought most of them began as messages with no place to be sent, pointing to a lack of feedback channels.

qa.q: What other approach could help catch problems early?
qa.a: Someone could read new public posts each morning and pass real issues to the team, so problems are met before they grow.

qa.q: How might a user with a problem see the new form?
qa.a: The user would have a clear place to send it and could expect a same-day reply, so there is less need to complain in public.

grounding: Shows a team adding a support form, a public changelog and faster replies after a public complaint episode.

subtype: Approach: clarifying what the mentee needs [Thinking]
passage:
Hi Seema,

Thanks for asking me to mentor you. Before I say yes to a plan, can I ask a few things? Where do you want to be a year from now? What has been hardest so far? I had planned to send you a list of technical topics, but after our call I noticed you hardly mentioned coding at all. You said you freeze in interviews and that three campus rounds went badly. So maybe what you need most is practice answering out loud, not more lectures from me. If you're up for it, we could do a mock interview next Saturday, and I'll ask you to send me two questions you dread. Tell me if that's not what you had in mind.

Anirban

qa.q: What did Seema say happens in interviews?
qa.a: Seema said Seema freezes in interviews, and three campus rounds went badly.

qa.q: What did Anirban believe Seema needed at first, and why did that view change?
qa.a: Anirban first planned a list of technical topics, but changed course because Seema hardly mentioned coding and talked about freezing in interviews.

qa.q: What could Anirban add to the mock interviews?
qa.a: Anirban could suggest Seema record the practice answers and listen back together, since hearing them helps show where the freezing starts.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on receiving this email?
qa.a: Seema would probably feel relieved and listened to, since Anirban asked before planning, though maybe nervous about the mock interview. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young engineer asking about goals and challenges before agreeing to mentor and realising that interview practice matters more than technical lectures.

subtype: Approach: setting a simple recurring schedule [Action]
passage:
Hi Gurleen,

I'm glad to be your mentor, and here's what I'd suggest so neither of us keeps rescheduling. Forty minutes on video, every other Sunday at 11. The Friday before, I'll send a short agenda with two or three items, and you add one of yours. At the end of each session we agree on one small task to finish before the next, something that fits into a week, like tidying one section of your portfolio or asking a senior for feedback. Our first is the 14th, the second the 28th. If a Sunday doesn't work, tell me by Thursday and we'll move it by a day, but we'll keep the rhythm. Does that feel manageable alongside your exams?

Naveen

qa.q: How long is each session, and how often do they meet?
qa.a: Each session is forty minutes, held every other Sunday.

qa.q: What does Naveen hope to avoid by proposing a fixed rhythm?
qa.a: Naveen hopes to avoid constant rescheduling, wanting steady progress that neither person has to chase.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if Gurleen keeps missing the small task?
qa.a: Naveen could ask what got in the way and make the task smaller, since a task that fits the week is more likely to be done.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel about the plan alongside exams?
qa.a: Gurleen would probably feel relieved that it is light and predictable, especially as Naveen asks if it is manageable.

grounding: Shows a mentor proposing forty-minute meetings on a fixed rota with an agenda sent beforehand and one small task at the end of each session.

subtype: Approach: giving answers instead of guiding [Pitfall]
passage: Coordinator's note, mentoring programme, three sessions observed. In session one Keerthana brought a failing spreadsheet formula and Nikita fixed it in two minutes, explaining nothing. Session two: a different sheet, the same kind of error, fixed by Nikita again. Keerthana thanked Nikita warmly and left with a working file. Session three: Keerthana arrived with that kind of problem a third time and said, 'Can you just do it? I always get it wrong.' Nikita did. Both left smiling, yet nothing had changed in what Keerthana could do alone. I spoke to Nikita afterwards, gently, and suggested asking Keerthana what she'd try first next time. Nikita said, 'I thought fast answers were the kindest thing.'

qa.q: How many sessions did the coordinator observe?
qa.a: The coordinator observed three sessions.

qa.q: Why did Nikita fix every problem?
qa.a: Nikita cared about helping Keerthana and believed fast answers were the kindest thing, so fixing each problem felt like being kind.

qa.q: What could Nikita do differently next session?
qa.a: Nikita could ask Keerthana what she would try first and let her attempt it, stepping in only with a small hint.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel about her own ability after three sessions?
qa.a: Keerthana probably still feels unsure and dependent, since she says 'I always get it wrong', grateful but not more confident.

grounding: Shows a mentor solving every problem for the mentee, who gets quick results but does not learn to think and returns with the same kind of problem.

subtype: Approach: asking questions to build thinking [Thinking]
passage: I'm Tara, and my desk faces the small meeting corner where Ishita meets Dilnaz on Wednesdays. Last week Dilnaz arrived stuck on a slow report page. I expected Ishita to type the fix. Instead Ishita asked, 'What have you tried?' Dilnaz listed two things. 'What else could it be?' Dilnaz named three options, hesitating. 'And if you chose the second one, how might it go wrong?' Dilnaz went quiet, then said, 'It could hide the real problem.' Ishita nodded and asked which option to test first. Twenty minutes later Dilnaz was typing alone. I can't say whether it felt frustrating or exciting to Dilnaz, but Dilnaz left with the answer and a small grin.

qa.q: How many options did Dilnaz name?
qa.a: Dilnaz named three options.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have been feeling when going quiet?
qa.a: Dilnaz was possibly uncertain and concentrating hard, and the small grin at the end suggests some satisfaction.

qa.q: What could Ishita do if Dilnaz stayed stuck?
qa.a: Ishita could give a small hint about where to look, without solving it, since a nudge keeps the thinking with Dilnaz.

qa.q: How might Tara have seen Ishita's way of helping?
qa.a: Tara expected a typed fix, so was probably surprised and interested in how much Dilnaz did alone.

grounding: Shows a mentor asking what has been tried, what the options are and how each might fail so the mentee reasons through the problem.
